newsitem.title: GERMANY: Krupp-Maastricht allows leeway on fiscal criteria.
newsitem.headline: Krupp-Maastricht allows leeway on fiscal criteria.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said on Monday the Maastricht Treaty allowed European Union nations some leeway to overshoot the reference levels set for public debt and the budget deficit.
The Treaty included clauses allowing countries to exceed the levels in exceptional circumstances or if they were reducing their debt at a sufficient pace, Krupp said.
These clauses were likely to be taken into account when assessing which EU countries qualified for monetary union, scheduled to start in January 1, 1999, Krupp said.

"This would not endanger stability. It would be desirable if the content of the Treaty were acknowledged in Germany," Krupp said according to the text of a speech made available ahead of delivery at a conference.

Doubts about whether Germany can qualify for monetary union have grown following recent forecasts that its budget deficit will exceed the reference level of three percent of GDP in 1997, the key year for deciding which nations can join.

Krupp said it was strange that public debate in Germany focused on the fiscal reference levels, whose significance was controversial, rather than on the inflation, interest rate and exchange rate criteria under which a sufficient number of countries had already achieved convergence.
"In the case of the fiscal reference levels the Treaty does not require nations to hit the spot exactly," Krupp said.
He also said: "Using the clauses which are expressly laid down in the Treaty is in keeping with the Treaty and in line with a strict application of the Treaty."
But he added that the clauses were not so "stretchable" that all EU countries could resort to them.
The second of the two fiscal criteria sets a reference level of 60 percent of GDP for a nation's public debt.
Krupp also said a comparison of bond yields revealed that financial markets regarded France, Belgium, Austria and the Netherlands as sure to launch monetary union with Germany.

"Long-term capital market rates in European partner countries which are roughly equivalent to the German level mean that market participants do not demand a risk premium because they expect these countries to belong to monetary union in 1999 along with Germany," Krupp said.
"Alongside countries like Belgium, Austria and the Netherlands the capital markets also see France as being among the certain launchers of monetary union," Krupp said.
French bond yields had in recent months been hovering around German yields and had at times even been below them, Krupp said.
He warned that the stability of the Euro would be put in doubt if the EU departed from the criteria to allow a large number of countries to join monetary union.

Delaying the launch to allow more countries to take part would ease pressure on less stability-conscious countries to fight inflation, cause uncertainty over whether monetary union would go ahead at all, and lead to an appreciation of the mark with resulting job losses, Krupp said.
"Protectionist tendencies would be strengthened," Krupp added.

Krupp also said that the rate at which the currencies of monetary union members are converted to the Euro should not be based on exchange rates at the end of 1998 because these could be distorted by chance.
The average exchange rate over a longer period of time could serve as a basis for conversion, or the central rates set in the present European Monetary System could be used, Krupp said.
"The type of conversion and its timely announcement could stabilise the expectations of market participants," Krupp said.
Krupp is president of the state central bank of Hamburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Schleswig-Holstein.
--David Crossland, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
